analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to prove and explain fairness when AI decides jobs, credit, housing, or insurance.
analysis.headline: The bill was never taken up: it sat in the Senate Commerce Committee from December 17, 2020 until the Congress ended on January 3, 2021, with no cosponsors and no committee action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would regulate companies that use algorithms — machine learning, advanced statistics, or artificial intelligence — to decide who gets a job, a loan, an apartment, health insurance, or other important opportunities. Companies could not act on decisions the Federal Trade Commission deems unfair; they would have to keep detailed records of how their algorithms work, tell people when an algorithm was used against them, and let people see and correct the data used and ask for a reevaluation. The FTC would study the industry and enforce the rules, and universities could get $10 million a year in research grants on fair data analytics. The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday people who are screened by software — job applicants scored by hiring algorithms, borrowers scored by credit models, renters and buyers screened by housing platforms, and people offered (or denied) insurance or education online. They would gain the right to know an algorithm judged them, see the data in plain language, fix wrong data, and ask the FTC to review an unfair decision, with civil penalties for companies that violate the rules [S3]. People in groups that algorithms often treat differently — by race, sex, age, disability, ZIP code, or other proxies — would gain the most, since the bill targets exactly those effects [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Bans companies from acting on an algorithmic decision about jobs, credit, housing, insurance, or education that the FTC finds unfair, and lets the FTC count bias against protected groups and emotional distress as real consumer injury when judging unfairness.

Gives individuals the right to be told when an algorithm was used against them, to see the data about themselves in a format a reasonable person can understand, to submit corrections, and to request a reevaluation based on the corrected data.

Requires companies to keep a five-year audit trail — the data used, how the model was built and tested for discriminatory effects across subgroups, and the result — and to turn it over to the FTC, which reviews it confidentially so trade secrets stay protected.

Directs the FTC to study how companies across industries build and use these algorithms — including whether they use race, religion, disability, criminal history, or proxies for them — report to Congress for six years, and refer suspected violations of federal anti-discrimination laws to the right agency.
Authorizes $10 million a year for six years in research grants at the National Institute of Standards and Technology for fair, accountable, and transparent data analytics.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that rely on algorithmic screening — tech platforms, banks and lenders, insurers, landlords and housing platforms, and employers — would bear the cost of building audit trails, testing for discriminatory effects, notifying individuals, handling correction and reevaluation requests, and FTC enforcement, including possible civil penalties [S3]. Compliant firms could face rivals that quietly keep using cheaper, unexamined models, though enforcement applies to all covered entities [S3].

drawbacks.text: Compliance would be costly, especially for small lenders, landlords, and employers who use off-the-shelf scoring tools and cannot easily document five years of training data, model versions, and bias tests — and the FTC must work with other agencies to reduce duplicative burdens, which the bill itself acknowledges as a real risk.

The bill does not require companies to reveal the algorithm itself, carving out trade secrets, and it exempts online advertisements and search results entirely from the individual-notification requirement — leaving some of the most common and least transparent algorithmic sorting largely outside its core protections.

'Unfairness' would be judged largely case-by-case by the FTC using the Federal Trade Commission Act standard, so outcomes would depend heavily on how the commission of the day defines unfair algorithmic decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real and targeted at a genuine, growing harm — automated decisions that people cannot see, question, or correct in hiring, credit, housing, and insurance. The strongest honest objection is compliance cost: documenting algorithms and handling correction requests would fall hard on small businesses, and the ad/search carve-out blunts the bill for some of the most pervasive algorithmic sorting. On balance, the benefits to people judged by black-box systems outweigh the costs, and the trade-secret protection plus confidential FTC review addresses the main intellectual-property objection the bill itself flags.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the final weeks of the 116th Congress and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Coons introduced the Algorithmic Fairness Act of 2020 on December 17, 2020 — 17 days before the end of the 116th Congress.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, and no further action was taken.
No senator cosponsored the bill, and it received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that use algorithmic tools to screen job applicants, borrowers, renters, and insurance customers are better off: they face no audit-trail, disclosure, or unfairness requirements, and no FTC enforcement or civil penalties. People screened by those systems gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: There was no vote and no second sponsor of either party, so the record shows only that a lone Democrat introduced the bill and no one else joined; the partisan shape of any opposition was never tested.

industries.note: The bill covers anyone whose algorithms decide access to jobs, credit, housing, insurance, or education — including common carriers and nonprofits — and would force these firms to document, test, and explain their models, with civil penalties for unfair decisions. Their interest in avoiding these costs runs against people's interest in fair, explainable decisions.

Online ads and search results are algorithmic eligibility determinations under the bill, but are explicitly exempt from the individual-notification requirement — a carve-out that leaves the sector largely untouched while other firms bear the compliance load.

The bill expressly pulls banks and savings institutions into FTC jurisdiction for algorithmic eligibility decisions about credit, adding audit-trail, notice, and correction duties and possible civil penalties on top of existing fair-lending law.
Algorithms deciding health insurance eligibility or cost are squarely covered; insurers would face fairness standards, notification duties, and FTC review of their models.

industries.industry: Employers and housing providers using screening algorithms
industries.note: Employment and housing decisions made by algorithmic tools would trigger the bill's substantive and procedural fairness requirements, and suspected discrimination would be referred to enforcement agencies.
The bill authorizes $10 million a year for six years in NIST grants for research into fair, accountable, and transparent data analytics.
